$doc: THE DISPATCH SURFACE — one declaration, two shells (#339).
Both shells marshal every post-boot .NET entry through a single serial lane.
Each method below declares whether it RETURNS IMMEDIATELY after queueing work
(fire-and-forget) or BLOCKS the caller until the work completes (blocking).
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: dispatchHostEvent existed in both shells, spelled
identically, and blocked in one. The Swift body was written for the deep-link
caller, where Android uses dispatchHostEventAndWait; the LIFECYCLE caller was
later pointed at the same method. On a device the permission sheet raises a
lifecycle event while an async host call holds the lane, and the app dies.
No name generator could have caught it -- the names match perfectly and the
BEHAVIOUR does not.
WHAT THE PIN CHECKS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT: DispatchSurfaceDriftTests asserts
each shell declares the methods listed here and that each method's LANE CALL
matches its declared semantics. It reads SOURCE. It does not observe blocking
at runtime -- a genuinely behavioural cross-shell pin would need a JVM test and
an XCTest that agree with each other, which is itself an unpinned twin.
TO ADD A METHOD: add it here, implement it in both shells, and run the pin. If
it genuinely belongs to one shell only, give it a `platforms` list AND a
`reason` -- asymmetry is allowed, silence is not.
COVERAGE LIMIT: the drift pin classifies the FIRST declaration of a name it
finds in each runtime source -- a diverging SECOND overload of an
already-declared name is not compared.
COMPLETENESS: `ignored` below is the OTHER half of the guard. Any method
whose name starts with `dispatch` and is declared in either runtime source
must appear either in `methods` above or in `ignored` below, each entry
carrying a `reason` -- a `dispatch*` method nobody mentions is invisible to
the pin by construction, which is the exact false-green route #339 exposed.

methods.name: dispatchEvent
methods.doc: A UI event from a control target. Non-zero rc routes to onError.

methods.name: dispatchEventAndWait
methods.reason: Consumed only by InspectorHost, a JVM-only developer tool with no iOS counterpart. Requiring a Swift twin would manufacture dead code to satisfy a guard.

methods.name: dispatchHostEvent
methods.doc: A host-initiated event. LIFECYCLE uses this. #339 is what happens when it blocks.

methods.name: dispatchHostEventAndWait
methods.doc: Deep-link and back: the caller needs the rc and needs frames applied before it returns.

ignored.name: dispatchCore
ignored.reason: Private ABI-marshalling helper shared by each shell's dispatchEvent overloads (builds the FlatJson args and crosses blazornative_dispatch_event) -- not itself a dispatch-surface entry point. The drift pin's own one-hop delegate resolver already follows into it when classifying a delegating declaration.

ignored.name: dispatchEventBlocking
ignored.reason: Test seam: runs dispatchEvent's marshalling INLINE on the calling thread and returns the raw rc, so JVM/XCTest assertions can read it directly. Production always dispatches through the async dispatchEvent -- the lane is the threading contract, not this seam.

ignored.name: dispatchHostEventUnchecked
ignored.reason: Test seam reachable with an ARBITRARY (possibly malformed) name so the rc-3 path stays testable; dispatchHostEvent (the enum overload) delegates to it for every production call, and NoProductionShellSource_CallsTheHostEventSeamsDirectly enforces that no other production code calls it directly. Swift's fire-and-forget path has no equivalent unchecked seam -- Swift's dispatchHostEvent has no delegate to hide behind.

ignored.name: dispatchHostEventBlocking
ignored.reason: Test seam: runs dispatchHostEvent's marshalling INLINE on the calling thread and returns the raw rc (HostEventTest.kt asserts the 0/1/2/3 contract directly). Production uses the fire-and-forget dispatchHostEvent (lifecycle) or the blocking dispatchHostEventAndWait (back) -- never this seam.
